stem:
Which of the following groups contain only biodegradable items?

(a) Grass, flowers and leather

(b) Grass, wood and plastic

(c) Fruit-peels, cake and lime-juice

(d) Cake, wood and grass
solution:
**(a), (c) and (d)** all contain only biodegradable items.

- (a) Grass, flowers and leather — all of natural origin, all broken down by micro-organisms.
- (c) Fruit-peels, cake and lime-juice — all food matter, readily decomposed.
- (d) Cake, wood and grass — again all organic and degradable.

**(b) is the odd one out**, because it contains **plastic**. Plastic is human-made and no enzyme acts on it, so it is non-biodegradable and the group is not made only of biodegradable items.
groundedIn: §13.2.2 — enzymes are specific, so human-made materials like plastics are not broken down by bacteria or saprophytes.

stem: Which of the following constitute a food-chain?
solution:
A food chain is a series of organisms in which each one is eaten by the next, so it must run from a **producer** through successive **consumers**.

- (A) Grass, wheat and mango — all three are producers. Nothing eats anything.
- **(B) Grass, goat and human** — grass (producer) \(\rightarrow\) goat (herbivore) \(\rightarrow\) human (consumer). A genuine chain.
- (C) Goat, cow and elephant — all three are herbivores at the same trophic level.
- (D) Grass, fish and goat — a fish does not eat grass on land and a goat does not eat fish; there is no feeding relationship.
groundedIn: §13.1.1 Food Chains and Webs — a food chain is the series of organisms through which food and energy are transferred, level by level.

stem: Which of the following are environment-friendly practices?

options.label: A
options.text: Carrying cloth-bags to put purchases in while shopping

options.label: B
options.text: Switching off unnecessary lights and fans

options.label: C
options.text: Walking to school instead of getting your mother to drop you on her scooter

solution:
Each of the three practices helps the environment in a different way:

- Carrying a **cloth bag** avoids plastic bags, which are non-biodegradable and persist in the environment.
- **Switching off unnecessary lights and fans** saves electricity, and so reduces the fuel burnt and the pollution produced to generate it.
- **Walking instead of riding** avoids burning petrol and the exhaust gases that come with it.

Since all three are environment-friendly, the answer is **all of the above**.
groundedIn: §13.2 and §13.2.2 — how our activities affect the environment, and reducing the waste we generate.

stem: What will happen if we kill all the organisms in one trophic level?
solution:
Removing an entire trophic level breaks the food chain and unbalances the whole ecosystem, in both directions at once:

- **The level above it starves.** Its food supply is gone, so those organisms die out or are forced to migrate.
- **The level below it multiplies unchecked.** Nothing is eating it any more, so its population explodes and it overgrazes or overconsumes the level below *that*.

For example, killing all the herbivores in a grassland would leave the carnivores with nothing to eat, while the grass would grow without limit.

Because the components of an ecosystem are interdependent, the disturbance does not stay local — it travels through every level, and the ecosystem may not be able to recover.
groundedIn: §13.1.1 — the interdependence of trophic levels and the transfer of energy along a food chain.

stem: Will the impact of removing all the organisms in a trophic level be different for different trophic levels? Can the organisms of any trophic level be removed without causing any damage to the ecosystem?
solution:
**Yes, the impact differs by level.**

- Removing the **producers** is the most catastrophic. Every other level ultimately depends on them for energy, so the whole ecosystem collapses.
- Removing the **herbivores** leaves the producers to grow unchecked and starves the carnivores above.
- Removing the **top carnivores** lets the level below them increase sharply, which then overgrazes the level below that.

**No — no trophic level can be removed without damage.** The components of an ecosystem are interdependent, and every level both supplies the one above and controls the one below. Removing any of them unbalances the system.

The one apparent exception is worth stating carefully: removing top carnivores does not starve anything above them, since nothing is above them — but it still causes damage, by letting their prey multiply without control.
groundedIn: §13.1.1 — the interdependence of the components of an ecosystem and the energy loss between trophic levels.

stem: What is biological magnification? Will the levels of this magnification be different at different levels of the ecosystem?
solution:
**Biological magnification** is the progressive build-up of harmful, non-degradable chemicals — pesticides, for instance — in the bodies of organisms as they pass along a food chain.

The chemicals are sprayed on crops, wash into the soil and water, and are absorbed by plants or taken in by animals. Because they cannot be broken down or excreted, they accumulate at every step.

**Yes, the level of magnification differs at different levels.** It is lowest in the producers and rises at each successive trophic level, being **highest at the top of the food chain**. Since human beings occupy the top level in any food chain, the maximum concentration of these chemicals accumulates in our bodies — which is why our food grains, vegetables, fruits and meat all carry varying amounts of pesticide residue, and why washing does not always remove them.
groundedIn: §13.1.1 — 'As these chemicals are not degradable, these get accumulated progressively at each trophic level. As human beings occupy the top level in any food chain, the maximum concentration of these chemicals get accumulated in our bodies. This phenomenon is known as biological magnification.'

stem: What are the problems caused by the non-biodegradable wastes that we generate?
solution:
- **They persist in the environment.** No biological process breaks them down, so plastics, glass and metals accumulate as litter and remain for decades.
- **They enter food chains and are biologically magnified.** Non-degradable chemicals such as pesticides pass from soil and water into plants and animals and become more concentrated at each trophic level, with human beings receiving the most.
- **They harm animals directly.** Discarded plastic is swallowed by cattle and other animals and can kill them.
- **They choke drains and water bodies**, causing water-logging and creating breeding grounds for mosquitoes.
- **They reduce soil fertility** and block the movement of water and air through the soil.
groundedIn: §13.2.2 — non-biodegradable substances 'may be inert and simply persist in the environment for a long time or may harm the various members of the eco-system'; magnification is from §13.1.1.

stem: If all the waste we generate is biodegradable, will this have no impact on the environment?
solution:
**No — it would still have an impact.** Biodegradable is not the same as harmless.

- Decomposition takes **time**. If waste is generated faster than micro-organisms can break it down, it still piles up.
- Rotting organic matter releases **foul smells and gases** such as methane, ammonia and hydrogen sulphide, polluting the air. Methane is also a greenhouse gas.
- Heaps of decomposing waste **attract flies, mosquitoes and rats**, which spread disease.
- Decomposition **consumes oxygen**. When large amounts of biodegradable waste enter a water body, the oxygen dissolved in the water is used up and aquatic life suffocates.

So the impact would certainly be **smaller** than with non-biodegradable waste, but it would not be zero. Proper management — composting, and not generating waste faster than it can be broken down — is still needed.
groundedIn: §13.2.2 Managing the Garbage we Produce, and the distinction drawn there between biodegradable and non-biodegradable substances.

stem: Why is damage to the ozone layer a cause for concern? What steps are being taken to limit this damage?
solution:
**Why it is a concern.** The ozone layer high in the atmosphere shields the surface of the earth from the Sun's **ultraviolet radiation**. UV radiation is highly damaging to living organisms — in human beings it is known to cause **skin cancer**. If the layer thins, more of this radiation reaches the ground and harms organisms at every level of every ecosystem.

**What caused the damage.** The amount of ozone began to drop sharply in the 1980s, and the cause was traced to synthetic chemicals, especially **CFCs (chlorofluorocarbons)**, which were widely used as refrigerants and in fire extinguishers.

**Steps being taken.** In 1987 the **United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP)** succeeded in forging an agreement to freeze CFC production at 1986 levels. Since then CFCs have been progressively phased out, and manufacturers worldwide now make CFC-free refrigerators and aerosols.
groundedIn: §13.2.1 Ozone Layer and How it is Getting Depleted — the UV-shielding role of ozone, the CFC cause, and the 1987 UNEP agreement.
